title: MSK Disorders: Lesson Route and Retrieval
series: BTEC L3 Applied Science · Unit 8 · A.P2

slides.heading: Musculoskeletal Disorders
slides.sub: How a change in tissue can alter movement and function
slides.vo: Welcome to this JD Science lesson for Unit 8 Learning Aim A. We are focusing on musculoskeletal disorders — and specifically on how a change in tissue can alter movement and function.

slides.heading: Retrieval — no notes
items: 2. Name one type of joint movement.
3. Name one structure that protects a joint.
slides.vo: Begin with three minutes of silent retrieval. Without notes, write one bone, one type of joint movement, and one structure that protects a joint. This warms up the knowledge we will stretch in the rest of the lesson.

slides.heading: Where this lesson goes

steps.d: Build a four-column table from the information sheet
See the osteoarthritis chain, then sort by tissue
Prove you can explain tissue change to movement

slides.vo: Here is the route. First you read and encode. Then we model osteoarthritis and sort disorders by tissue. Next comes guided case practice. Finally you produce independent evidence that links tissue change to movement.

slides.heading: Explain the chain, not just the label
slides.body: Disorder → tissue change → effect on movement → management
slides.vo: Your success criterion is clear: do not stop at naming the disorder. Explain the chain — which tissue changes, how that alters movement, and what management targets that change.

title: MSK Disorders: Read and Encode
series: BTEC L3 Applied Science · Unit 8 · A.P2

slides.heading: Meet the disorders
slides.sub: Read with a purpose before you apply
slides.vo: This section is purposeful reading. You will turn the information sheet into a clear four-column table so every disorder is ready to use later in sorting and cases.

slides.heading: Four columns to fill
slides.vo: Set up four columns: disorder, tissue affected, effect on movement, and management. Those four ideas are the language of Learning Aim A.

slides.heading: How to work
items: Seven minutes of silent individual reading
Complete at least six of the twelve disorders
Paraphrase in your own words — do not copy
Keep your information sheet out for the whole lesson
slides.vo: Work silently for seven minutes. Aim for at least six of the twelve disorders. Paraphrase rather than copy, and keep the sheet available — you will need it for sorting and cases.

slides.heading: Encoding makes retrieval reliable
slides.body: A tidy table lets you sort by tissue and explain cases without guessing.
slides.vo: Encoding now pays off later. When you sort by tissue or tackle a case, you will retrieve from your table instead of guessing from memory.

title: MSK Disorders: Osteoarthritis Model
series: BTEC L3 Applied Science · Unit 8 · A.P2

slides.heading: From tissue change to movement
slides.sub: Osteoarthritis as a four-part explanation chain
slides.vo: Watch a strong model answer using osteoarthritis. The goal is to explain why movement changes — not only to list symptoms.

slides.heading: Structure → Function → Movement → Management

steps.d: Articular cartilage thins and roughens at the joint surface
Smooth, low-friction gliding is reduced; bone ends stress more
Pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion limit loading and gait
Exercise, weight management, analgesia; surgery if severe

slides.vo: Structure: cartilage thins and roughens. Function: low-friction gliding falls and bone ends take more stress. Movement: pain and stiffness cut range of motion and alter gait. Management targets that chain — activity, load, pain relief, and surgery if needed.

slides.heading: Do not stop at symptoms

left.d: Osteoarthritis causes joint pain and stiffness.

right.d: Cartilage wear raises friction, so pain and stiffness reduce range of motion and loading.

slides.vo: A weak answer only names pain and stiffness. A strong answer links cartilage wear to friction, then to limited movement. That is the standard for A.P2.

slides.heading: Reuse this chain for every disorder
slides.body: Ask: which tissue changed, and how does that change movement?
slides.vo: Reuse this chain for every disorder you meet. Always ask which tissue changed, and how that change alters movement.

title: MSK Disorders: Tissue Sort
series: BTEC L3 Applied Science · Unit 8 · A.P2

slides.heading: Tissue explains the symptoms
slides.vo: Now sort the twelve disorders into four tissue groups. The group you choose should explain the symptoms you expect.

slides.heading: Four groups by primary tissue change
slides.vo: Bone mineralisation covers osteoporosis, osteomalacia, rickets and Paget's. Infection or abnormal growth covers osteomyelitis and bone tumours. Muscle or motor control covers muscular dystrophy and motor neurone disease. Joint and alignment covers osteoarthritis, hip dysplasia, scoliosis and hypermobility.

slides.heading: Why is MND under motor control?
slides.body: Motor neurone disease damages the signal to muscle, not the muscle fibre as the primary tissue.
slides.vo: Check: motor neurone disease sits under motor control because the primary failure is the nerve signal to muscle, not a primary muscle-fibre disease like dystrophy.

title: MSK Disorders: Case Practice
series: BTEC L3 Applied Science · Unit 8 · A.P2

slides.heading: Check the explanation, not just the label
slides.sub: Short cases · finger show · full chain
slides.vo: Use short cases to practise. Show fingers for how complete your explanation is: all four parts, two parts, or the disorder name only.

slides.heading: Post-surgical bone pain, swelling and fever

points.d: Bone and bone marrow — infection and inflammation
Pain and swelling limit loading and range
Antibiotics and surgical debridement when needed

slides.vo: Case A: post-surgical bone pain with swelling and fever points to osteomyelitis. Infected bone and marrow cause pain that limits loading. Management is antibiotics, with debridement if required.

slides.heading: Child with bowed legs and vitamin D deficiency

points.d: Growing bone and growth plates — poor mineralisation
Softened bones bow; gait and alignment change
Vitamin D and calcium; address deficiency cause

slides.vo: Case B: a child with bowed legs and low vitamin D suggests rickets. Growing bones mineralise poorly, soften, and bow under weight, changing gait. Management restores vitamin D and calcium.

slides.heading: Name · tissue · movement · management
slides.body: If you only name the disorder, upgrade your answer before you move on.
slides.vo: If you only name the disorder, upgrade the answer before moving on. Aim for name, tissue, movement effect, and management every time.

title: MSK Disorders: Hinge Question
series: BTEC L3 Applied Science · Unit 8 · A.P2

slides.heading: Prove the discriminating fact
slides.sub: One clue that forces the correct disorder
bullets: State why B must be right
slides.vo: Finish with a hinge question. The aim is to spot the single fact that forces the correct disorder and rules the others out.

slides.heading: Answer B — Rickets
slides.body: Defective mineralisation of growing bones and growth plates, often from vitamin D deficiency. Softened bones bow under body weight.
slides.vo: The correct answer is rickets. The discriminating clue is growing bones with poor mineralisation, so softened bone can bow under body weight.

slides.heading: Eliminate with tissue logic

items.d: Density falls as resorption outpaces formation — not a growth-plate mineralisation problem.
Bacterial bone infection with inflammation — no infection signs in the stem.
Affects skeletal muscle fibres, not bone mineralisation.

slides.vo: Osteoporosis is about adult density balance, not growth-plate mineralisation. Osteomyelitis needs infection signs. Muscular dystrophy targets muscle fibres, not bone. Only rickets fits growing bones that soften and bow.

slides.heading: What single fact forced answer B?
slides.body: Write one sentence from your information sheet that made rickets unavoidable.
slides.vo: Exit ticket: write one sentence from your sheet that made rickets unavoidable. If you can state that discriminating fact, you are ready for independent evidence.
